solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Eccentric priest, not against a bit of tendentiousness, a rationalist (10, two words)

indicators.note: something eccentric is off-centre and odd, so the following word's letters are set in a strange new order
a bit of a word is just a small piece of it, here its opening letter

blocks.note: the word itself, to be rearranged
if you are not against something you are for it
its first letter

explanation.surface: An odd clergyman, sympathetic to slanted arguments, who nonetheless thinks of himself as a man of reason.
explanation.definitionFit: An esprit fort (French, 'strong spirit') is a freethinker who rejects received religious belief, i.e. a rationalist.

clue.text: Liqueur, almost the last of it, worthless, imbibed in company

indicators.note: 'it' points back to the clue's first word, and almost the last letter is the one just before the end
something imbibed is taken inside, so these letters go within the abbreviation that follows

blocks.note: its second-last letter, picked out through 'it'
a biblical term of contempt (Matthew 5:22) meaning empty-headed or worthless
standard abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: A drink nearly finished, its dregs no good, consumed among friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' refers back to the clue's first word, so the selection is made from Liqueur itself. RACA is obscure: Chambers glosses it as worthless.
explanation.definitionFit: Curacao is an orange-flavoured liqueur named after the Caribbean island where its bitter oranges grow.

clue.text: Ransack channel for handy menial in sea-food joint?

blocks.note: to fish is to search or rummage through something
a gutter is a channel carrying water away

explanation.surface: A job advert for a kitchen helper: rummaging through drains in a fish restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition as playful: the worker is 'handy' because the job is done by hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A fish-gutter is a worker who cleans out fish, the sort of lowly job found in a seafood kitchen or processing plant.

clue.text: Surge following opening of farce, break from Shakespeare

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its very first letter

blocks.note: its first letter
a sudden surge or rush of water or people

explanation.surface: A wave of laughter after a comedy begins gives the audience relief from heavy Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' places the surge after the opening letter. 'From Shakespeare' marks the verb as one he used that has since died out.
explanation.definitionFit: Frush is a Shakespearean verb meaning to smash or batter, used in Troilus and Cressida, so it is an old word for break.

clue.text: Tasty barbecue item? Stop pinching one

indicators.note: to pinch something is to grip it, so the next letter is held inside

blocks.note: to stay is to stop or remain
a, as in a single one

explanation.surface: A delicious grilled morsel, and someone told to stop stealing one from the plate.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: satay is a dish, typically skewered and grilled, rather than one item.
explanation.definitionFit: Satay is Southeast Asian skewered meat grilled over coals and served with peanut sauce, a common barbecue food.

clue.text: Anything but forthright, disturbing the antis

indicators.note: to disturb is to throw out of order, so the following letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the words as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone evasive is upsetting the people who oppose them.
explanation.definitionFit: Hesitant means faltering and unwilling to commit, the opposite of being direct and outspoken.

clue.text: Booby – or another seabird

blocks.note: first meaning: a dupe or fool, someone easily tricked
second meaning: a common coastal bird; 'another' because a booby is itself a seabird

explanation.walkthrough: Booby reads as the tropical seabird, which is why the second half says 'another'; in fact it is the sense of a simpleton.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun gull means a person easily deceived, and it is also the name of a familiar grey-and-white marine bird.

clue.text: What you can get thinner from? Concoction of three girlfriend swallowed

definitions.text: What you can get thinner from

indicators.note: a concoction mixes ingredients up, so the letters of the next word are blended into a new order
whatever is swallowed ends up inside, so the word before it goes within the mixed letters

blocks.note: the word itself, to be rearranged
bint is British slang, now derogatory, for a girl or girlfriend

explanation.surface: A bartender's recipe for a thinner drink, mixed for three while a girlfriend gulps it down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thinner' suggests something less fat, but it is the paint solvent: turpentine was first obtained from this tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The terebinth is a Mediterranean tree whose resin yields turpentine, the classic solvent used for thinning paint.

clue.text: Colourful bird to be sold in marketplace

indicators.note: the phrase before it is placed in the middle of the word that follows

blocks.note: goods go for a price when they are sold
a tron is a Scottish public weighing machine, and by extension the marketplace where it stood

explanation.surface: A brightly plumaged bird up for sale at the market.
explanation.walkthrough: TRON is a Scots word Azed solvers meet often: the public weighbeam, then the place it stood.
explanation.definitionFit: Trogons are tropical forest birds famous for their vivid green, red and yellow plumage; the quetzal is one.

clue.text: What's poet read? This crafted with art maybe

indicators.note: something crafted is skilfully made from raw material, so the earlier words' letters are refashioned
the mix holds the answer together with the next word, so that word must be taken back out

blocks.note: the words as written, the raw material
taken as written; these letters are removed from the mix

explanation.surface: Asking what a poet recited, and answering that this piece was made with skill.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: 'This' (the answer) together with ART rearranges the letters of 'poet read', so the answer is what remains once ART is set aside.
explanation.definitionFit: 'This' stands for the answer itself, an epode, a lyric poem or the third part of an ode, which a poet would recite.

clue.text: Deity viewable by anyone immersed in shimmering rays

indicators.note: shimmering light wavers and shifts, so the letters of the next word move about
something immersed is plunged inside, so this letter goes within the others

blocks.note: U is the British film certificate for 'universal', a film anyone may watch
the word itself, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A god revealed to all, bathed in flickering sunbeams.
explanation.definitionFit: Surya is the Hindu sun god, a deity often pictured riding a chariot drawn by seven horses.

clue.text: Scrambling up tree, fourth of date palms

indicators.note: scrambling mixes things up, so these letters are thrown into a new order
only the letter in fourth position of the next word is kept

blocks.note: the words as written, to be rearranged
its fourth letter

explanation.surface: Climbing a tree to get at dates on the palms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Palms' looks like part of the scene with 'date' and 'tree', but it alone is the definition, a plant genus.
explanation.definitionFit: Euterpe is a genus of tropical American palms, including the acai palm; it shares its name with the Muse of music.

clue.text: Glass decorations giving one kicks round edge of tumbler

indicators.note: the edge of a word is a letter at its boundary, here the closing one
the word before it is wrapped round the letter that follows

blocks.note: someone who kicks a ball punts it
its last letter

explanation.surface: A drinking glass with ornaments, booted around by someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Prunts are blobs of glass applied to a vessel as ornament, often seen on old German drinking glasses.

clue.text: Decline a small drink, imbibing nothing

indicators.note: to imbibe is to take in, so the drink holds the next letter inside it

blocks.note: a drop is a small amount of drink
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Turning down even a tiny tipple, and drinking nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decline' reads as refuse, but it is the sense of sag or flag.
explanation.definitionFit: To droop is to sink or flag, losing vigour, which is one sense of decline.

clue.text: Large bill includes e.g. jigger for Oxford scholar

indicators.note: something that includes another holds it within, so the bill wraps round the next item

blocks.note: a bill is a printed notice; a large one is a poster
a jigger mast is the aftermost mast on some sailing vessels

explanation.surface: An outsize invoice listing a measure of spirits, sent to an Oxford academic.
explanation.walkthrough: A jigger is also a spirit measure, which the 'bill' encourages, but here it is a ship's mast.
explanation.definitionFit: At Merton College, Oxford, a scholar holding one of the college's portionist awards is traditionally called a postmaster.

clue.text: Poorly, in grip of scare, a disorderly mob? Och aye

indicators.note: disorderly means out of order, so the letters are rearranged
held in the grip of something means enclosed by it, so the first word goes inside

blocks.note: the words as written, to be rearranged
feeling poorly is being ill
surface padding: a Scottish exclamation flagging that the answer is a Scots word

explanation.surface: A sick person, frightened by an unruly crowd, with a Scottish exclamation tacked on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Och aye' tells the solver the answer is a Scots word; it gives no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Rascaille is an old Scots word for the rabble, the common rout or riff-raff, so a mob.

clue.text: Helm anchor? Check strain that's twisted sloop's rear

indicators.note: something twisted is bent out of shape, so the letters are reordered
the rear of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: CH is the chess abbreviation for check
the word itself, to be rearranged
its last letter, ignoring the possessive

explanation.surface: A sailing scene: the tiller, the anchor, a twisted rope under strain at the stern of a sloop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Helm' looks like the ship's steering gear, but it is the old word for a helmet, and what anchors a helmet runs under the chin.
explanation.definitionFit: A chinstrap holds a helmet (archaically a helm) securely on the head, so it anchors it.

clue.text: Moved away, having retired, directed inside

indicators.note: the word before it is placed within the earlier word

blocks.note: someone who has retired for the night is in bed
to direct someone somewhere is to send them

explanation.surface: Someone who left their post after retiring, having been told to stay at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' reads as stopped working, but here it means gone to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: To absent yourself is to take yourself off or stay away, so absented means withdrew.

clue.text: Players booed endlessly (and drunkenly) by character at front of stalls

indicators.note: without its end, so the word loses its final letter
a drunk staggers about, so the remaining letters lurch into a new order
the character at the front of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: the word itself, to be trimmed then rearranged
its first letter

explanation.surface: Actors jeered without pause by a tipsy theatregoer sitting in the front stalls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Players' suggests actors on a stage, but it means instruments: musicians and instruments alike can be called players in an orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: Oboes are woodwind instruments, and an oboe is also the name for an oboist, the musician who plays it.

clue.text: Items of oriental hosiery, a bit the worse for wear

indicators.note: something worse for wear is battered out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the words as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Eastern socks that are getting a little shabby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The worse for wear' fits socks so well that it hides its role as the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabi are Japanese ankle socks with a separate big toe, worn with sandals, so they are hosiery from the Far East.

clue.text: Curtain material? Sounds like something cat's caught in

indicators.note: says outright that the answer is pronounced like the phrase that follows

blocks.note: a tabby is a striped cat, and a net is something it might be caught in

explanation.surface: Wondering if a curtain fabric is what a cat might get tangled up in.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as an example: the fabric was used for curtains among other furnishings.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabbinet is a watered poplin fabric of silk and wool, used for upholstery and hangings such as curtains.

clue.text: Regular variation spoilt duet, except for the first, not so good

indicators.note: everything apart from the opening letter is kept, so that first letter goes
something spoilt has been messed up, so the remaining letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the word itself, to be trimmed then rearranged
ropy is British informal for poor or below par

explanation.surface: A performance that keeps varying because the duet went wrong apart from the opening, and wasn't up to much.
explanation.definitionFit: Eutropy is regular variation, specifically the systematic change in crystal form through a series of related chemical compounds.

clue.text: Favouring home that's about new? Jock's bang opposite

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the home goes round the next letter

blocks.note: if you favour something you are for it
a nest is a home
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Someone who prefers a house that feels fresh, and a Scot who is directly across the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jock' is British slang for a Scot, signalling a Scots word; 'bang' means exactly, as in bang on.
explanation.definitionFit: Fornenst is a Scots preposition meaning directly facing or over against, so exactly opposite.

clue.text: Odd pieces from Sicily (ruined) transported as mementos

indicators.note: odd pieces are the first, third, fifth and so on, taken from the words that follow
transported means carried off and moved about, so the kept letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth letters and so on

explanation.surface: Fragments from Sicilian ruins carried home as souvenirs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruined' sits in brackets as if a stage direction; it is half of the letter source, and the bracketed word is read on from Sicily.
explanation.definitionFit: Relics are objects kept in remembrance of a person, place or past time, which is what mementos are.

clue.text: Book 4 summarily includes English group of notes sung on same note

definitions.text: group of notes sung on same note

indicators.note: the abbreviation holds the next letter within it

blocks.note: Numbers is the fourth book of the Bible, abbreviated NUM
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A summary of a book's fourth chapter mentions plainsong sung on a single pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Summarily' means in shortened form, the usual abbreviation of the book of Numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: A neum is a sign in medieval plainsong notation, or a group of notes sung to one syllable.

clue.text: Needing to diet? Number going outside to be seen

indicators.note: the number leaves from the outer edges, so its letters are stripped from both ends of the phrase

blocks.note: ten is a number; its letters are split, one at the start and two at the end
the words as written; that the result runs through them is a coincidence of the deletion, not a hidden word

explanation.surface: A heavy person reluctant to go out in public.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove T from the front and EN from the end of TOBESEEN; the number is split across the outside of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone obese is seriously overweight, the condition in which a doctor would advise losing weight.

clue.text: Bored with pleasure, there being little left in bed

indicators.note: the letter goes in the middle of the word that follows

blocks.note: a base is a foundation or bed, as a road is laid on a bed
L is the abbreviation for left, and as a lone letter it is little

explanation.surface: Weary of indulgence, with not much life remaining and confined to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Blase describes someone so used to enjoyment that they are indifferent to it, unimpressed by pleasures.

clue.text: Climb in mountainous Caledonia

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the words that follow, running across their boundary

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: An ascent in the Scottish Highlands.
explanation.walkthrough: Caledonia is the old Latin name for Scotland, which makes the setting look like the point.
explanation.definitionFit: To scale a mountain or wall is to climb up it, so the verb is a straight synonym.

clue.text: Workman on roof maybe starting at bottom got going again

indicators.note: in a down clue, starting at the bottom means reading the word upwards

blocks.note: a tiler lays tiles, roof tiles for instance

explanation.surface: A roofer, working his way up from the lowest row, gets the job restarted.
explanation.definitionFit: Relit is the past tense of relight: a fire relit has been set burning once more, so restarted.

clue.text: Boards required for those digging protective ditches

blocks.note: first meaning: wooden platters for serving food
second meaning: people who excavate defensive earthworks

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as planks being needed to shore up a trench; boards here are serving platters.
explanation.definitionFit: A trencher is a flat wooden plate, and literally one who trenches, digging fortified ditches.

clue.text: Flat stage removed from outskirts of Herts location

indicators.note: the letters come off the outer edges of the town's name, leaving its middle

blocks.note: Stevenage is a town in Hertfordshire, the English county abbreviated Herts
the word itself, split as ST at the front and AGE at the back

explanation.surface: A level platform taken down at the edge of a Hertfordshire town.
explanation.definitionFit: Even means level and smooth, without bumps, which is one sense of flat.

clue.text: Rope from rear decapitated SA carnivore

indicators.note: losing its head, the word drops its first letter
read from the rear means read from the back to the front

blocks.note: a lariat is a lasso, a rope

explanation.surface: Lassoing a South American predator from behind before beheading it.
explanation.walkthrough: SA stands for South America here, not South Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: The tayra or taira is a tree-dwelling member of the weasel family found in Central and South American forests.

clue.text: Ultimate for artist having to share garret

indicators.note: the ultimate letter of a word is its final one

blocks.note: its last letter
to allot is to share out or apportion

explanation.surface: The final indignity for a struggling painter: having to share a cramped attic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Garret' calls up the starving artist's attic, which is why the artist seems to be part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tallot, or tallat, is a dialect word for a hayloft or the upper room of an outbuilding, so an attic.

clue.text: One bolting sword round sheath? No p-poet

indicators.note: says the stammered phrase after it is to be taken away from the earlier word
the sword goes round what is left of the other word

blocks.note: an epee is a fencing sword
a scabbard is a sword's sheath
a stammered poet, a b-bard, bard being a poet

explanation.surface: Someone running off with a sword in its sheath, and a stuttering poet told to stay out of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The stutter is the trick: 'p-poet' becomes B-BARD, and removing those letters from SCABBARD leaves SCA.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapee is a person who has escaped or broken free, so someone who has bolted.

clue.text: I'll be involved in long run – langlaufers follow it

indicators.note: to be involved in something is to be caught up within it

blocks.note: I'll is I will: the letter I is what will be placed
a lope is a long, easy bounding stride or run

explanation.surface: Someone joining a long run, along the trail cross-country skiers use.
explanation.walkthrough: A langlaufer is a cross-country skier, from German Langlauf, 'long run'.
explanation.definitionFit: A loipe is a prepared cross-country skiing track, the route that Nordic skiers travel along.

clue.text: Cent losing out to major currency, third going in fall, sad

indicators.note: one thing losing out to another is replaced by it
going means leaving, so the named letter is removed
says where the swap takes place, inside the following word

blocks.note: a descent is a fall
C is the abbreviation for cent
the pound sterling, a major world currency
the third letter of the currency

explanation.surface: A gloomy currency trader watching the cent lose out to the pound in a slump.
explanation.definitionFit: Despondent means dejected and without hope, which is a stronger form of sad.
